worksheet.title: Predict, Then Find
worksheet.subtitle: Predict the goal, run, find the bug
worksheet.learning_goal: I can predict the right answer, run the code, and find the script that does not match.

parts.title: Predict first, then check
parts.text: Good debuggers know what the answer SHOULD be before they run. Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag and should BOTH reach number 4. First PREDICT where each should land. Then run the code and find the one script that does NOT match your prediction.

parts.title: Predict the goal
parts.prompt: The goal is for both to reach 4. Before running, what number SHOULD each sprite land on? Bit: ____  Pixel: ____

parts.title: Run and find the off one
parts.prompt: Now run both. Bit (home 2, forward 2): ____  Pixel (home 1, forward 2): ____. Which sprite did NOT match your prediction?

parts.title: Find and fix
parts.prompt: What is the bug in the off script, and what is the fix? Pixel starts at 1 and needs 4, so its move should be forward ____. After the fix, does it match the goal?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When you predict the answer first, a bug is easy to spot: the script whose result does NOT match your prediction is the buggy one. Then you only have to find and fix that one. Here Pixel needed forward 3, not forward 2.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Debugging & Reading Code
teacher_guide.title: Predict, Then Find
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students combine prediction with debugging: predict the intended outcome (both reach 4), run the code, and use the mismatch to locate the bug (C3.2). Bit matches the prediction; Pixel does not (it lands on 3), so Pixel is the buggy script — fix it to 'forward 3'. Predicting first turns debugging into a quick match/no-match check.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: students write the predicted number (4) on a sticky note before running, then compare each sprite's result to it.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: predict — 'the goal is 4, so both SHOULD land on 4.' Write 4 down before running.
2. WE DO: run Bit (2 forward 2 → 4 — matches) and Pixel (1 forward 2 → 3 — does NOT match). 'Pixel is the bug.'
3. YOU DO: students find Pixel's fix — from 1 it needs forward 3 to reach 4 — and confirm it now matches.
4. Connect: 'Predict first; the script that does not match your prediction is where the bug is.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — both SHOULD land on the goal 4 (Bit 4, Pixel 4 if correct).
Ex 2 — Bit: 2 → forward 2 → 4 (matches). Pixel: 1 → forward 2 → 3 (does NOT match). Pixel is the off script.
Ex 3 — Pixel starts at 1 and needs 4, so its move should be forward 3. After the fix, Pixel lands on 4 and matches the goal.
Method note: the prediction (4) is the yardstick; the script whose run differs from it is the buggy one.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: changing the prediction to match the buggy result — commit the prediction first, in pen.
Common error: suspecting Bit — Bit matched the prediction, so it is correct; the mismatch is in Pixel.
Simplify: write the goal number above each sprite and compare its run to that number.
Extend: ask students to make up a different bug for Pixel that would still miss the goal, then fix it.
Success indicator: the child predicts 4, identifies Pixel as off, and fixes it to forward 3.
